problem.title: Electron accelerated across a parallel-plate gap
problem.text:
An electron is released from rest at the negative plate of a parallel-plate capacitor with a
potential difference of 100 V across a 2.0 cm gap. How fast is it moving when it reaches the
positive plate?

trajectory.integrator: RK4 (exact for constant acceleration; <0.5% phase error on cyclotron orbits at the sampled dt)

because.detail: An electron, with charge and mass fixed by nature rather than by the problem.
Two oppositely charged plates. Away from the edges the field between them is uniform, which makes this the standard way to produce a known constant field in a problem.
The surrounding medium and fields. Defaults are an idealised vacuum with no gravity, which is what textbook electrostatics problems assume -- stated here as an editable value instead of a footnote.

because.law_statement: Potential is potential energy per unit charge; the work to move a charge between two points is the charge times the potential difference.

because.law_label: Weight in a uniform gravitational field
because.law_statement: A body of mass m in a uniform gravitational field g experiences a force m*g directed along the field. Uniform is the right idealisation on a bench: g varies by less than a part in a million across a desk.

The net force on a body is the vector sum of the forces acting on it, each computed as if the others were absent. This is why an electric force and a weight can be derived independently and then added.
A scalar magnitude property is the Euclidean norm of its vector counterpart. Bookkeeping, not physics, but it must be cited like anything else so no trace step is unexplained.
The net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration.
While acceleration is constant, velocity is linear in time and displacement is quadratic; and v^2 = u^2 + 2*a*s eliminates time entirely.
